conversation.content:
Hello! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms feel their best emotionally after baby arrives. To get a clear picture of how things are going for you, I’ll be using a quick, 10-item questionnaire called the EPDS. It screens for depressive and anxiety symptoms that sometimes show up in the postpartum period, and it includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything we discuss is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no right or wrong answer, only what’s true for you. We’ll move through the questions at your pace, and if anything feels uncomfortable, we can pause or adjust. Ready to start? 

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even during the tough moments of new motherhood?

Honestly... I can’t remember the last time I laughed. Even when my husband tries to be funny—like when he put the diaper on backwards—I just kind of half-smiled and then felt guilty for not laughing. Nothing feels funny right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I’ve smiled a couple of times, but a real laugh? That hasn’t happened in the past week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much... I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat. I’ll think “I should enjoy this,” but the feeling never really comes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If she cries longer than usual, I’m sure it’s because I missed some cue or didn’t feed her right. When the laundry piles up or we run out of diapers, I tell myself I’m failing at the one job I’m supposed to be good at—being her mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

That happens a lot. I’ll be sitting with her while she’s napping and suddenly imagine she’s stopped breathing, or I’ll worry that the little rash on her cheek is something terrible. My heart races and I can’t settle until I check her three or four times, even though I know I’m probably overreacting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a wave hits me out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen. There’s no real reason; she’ll be sleeping peacefully and I’ll still feel like the room is closing in.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep, and just keeping her happy, it feels like I’m drowning a little. I manage to get the basics done, but I’m running on empty and it’s overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—going over everything I did wrong that day, worrying she’ll wake up any second. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do, I jolt awake at every little sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits with me, even when nothing in particular is wrong. I’ll look at her sweet face and still feel empty inside, and then I hate myself for not feeling happier when I have this beautiful baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes… three or four times this week. Yesterday it was while I was trying to get her to latch—she kept pulling away and I just broke down. I felt so useless, like I can’t even feed my own baby right.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

You've shared how the joy you expected after your baby's arrival has been replaced by a persistent heaviness-nothing feels funny or exciting, daily tasks feel overwhelming, and you carry a steady stream of self-criticism even when things go well. You described frightening waves of panic, nightly battles with racing thoughts, and frequent tears that leave you feeling depleted yet still pushing forward for your little one.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports no genuine laughter in the past week, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports clear loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" and gives multiple examples of feeling personally responsible for routine infant/ household issues, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, uncontrollable worries occurring "a lot" with physical anxiety symptoms</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden unexpected panic with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports difficulty coping "most days" and "running on empty," matching the "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual" level.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness, emotional emptiness despite positive circumstances, and self-criticism, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 23 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, recurrent tearfulness, psychomotor agitation (panic episodes), fatigue, and insomnia. You denied <med>self-harm ideation</med>, yet the intensity and persistence of other symptoms warrant immediate clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and medication compatible with breastfeeding if desired
3. Plan daily 15-minute «breathing room» where a support person cares for the baby while you rest, shower, or step outside; protecting small sleep stretches can lessen symptom severity
4. Use brief grounding techniques (slow breathing, naming five things you see) when sudden panic rises; keep emergency contacts on your phone for real-time support
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
6. Encourage open conversation with trusted family or friends about how you're feeling so they can offer practical help and emotional reassurance
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 1-wk postpartum

<sym> endorsed symptoms  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of laugh, anticipatory pleasure)  
- Daily pervasive low mood, frequent crying spells  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt over routine infant-care tasks  
- Unwarranted anxiety, catastrophic worries re infant safety  
- Episodic panic (chest tightness, breathlessness) without trigger  
- Subjective sense of “drowning,” difficulty coping  
- Initial insomnia and middle insomnia tied to ruminative worry  

<med> screening significance  
- Pattern consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety.  
- No self-harm ideation reported (denies item 10).  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, feeding difficulties, distressing intrusive worries.

Risk factors noted  
- Primiparous, early postpartum period, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, absence of mentioned support.

Observation  
Mother demonstrates multiple core features of postpartum mood/anxiety disorder; further clinical evaluation (diagnostic interview, psychosocial supports, safety plan) indicated. No acute safety concerns voiced at present.
